title: OA session weaver: idempotent request/response mapper for Chat Completions compatibility
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Implement a compatibility layer called 'session weaver' that maps incoming OpenAI Chat Completions (v1/chat/completions) requests into Redwood's internal request model and reconstructs responses (including streaming chunks, tool/function calls, and structured outputs) back into OpenAI-shaped envelopes. The goal is to support legacy clients without requiring them to migrate, while preserving Redwood runtime features: continuous batching, KV cache, model fallbacks, and token-level telemetry. This ticket focuses on request/response mapping semantics, idempotency/session stitching for partial/streamed events, and graceful fallbacks for tool-calling sequences that require buffering to maintain JSON integrity.
acceptance_criteria: Legacy OA chat clients receive responses indistinguishable in shape from upstream OpenAI chat-completions (status codes, streaming SSE frames, function call JSON) for a representative set of test prompts
Streaming responses that do not include function calls must remain token-level streamed with <100ms additional latency in the happy path compared to native Redwood streaming

Requests with function/tool calling produce a single well-formed function call JSON event in the final response and an explicit 'tool-invoked' event in streaming mode when using OpenAI-compatible streaming clients
Idempotent replay: re-sent requests with identical client-provided request_id are detected and deduplicated within a 5 minute window
Automated test coverage: unit tests covering mapping rules, integration test against legacy SDK, and an E2E demo that exercises tool calls and structured output preservation
implementation_notes: Mapping approach: two-layer translator. Inbound translator normalizes OA request fields (messages, system/user/assistant roles, max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop) to Redwood internal shape. Outbound translator reconstructs SSE event frames and final JSON following OA ordering rules.

Idempotency: prefer client-supplied 'x-request-id' header. If absent, generate hashed session key from client IP, model, and first-message fingerprint. Store short-lived dedupe entries in Redis with 5-minute TTL.

Tool-calling: when runtime detects a tool call in generation, buffer until top-level function call object is complete to produce a single function_call event for OA clients. This implies a buffering path for tool sequences; latency trade-off documented below.

Streaming trade-off: two modes. Token-forward streaming (low-latency) for plain text responses; buffered streaming for streams containing structured JSON/tool calls to ensure JSON validity and single function_call emission. Use a header flag in the event envelope to signal buffered mode to downstream proxies.

Telemetry: emit token-level and event-level metrics with a compat tag. Add new traces: compat.session_id, compat.mode (streaming|buffered), compat.tool_call=true/false. Update console dashboard to show compat error rates and p95 latency.

Backward-compat: ensure older clients that rely on chunk ordering and 'finish_reason' semantics get identical finish_reason values (stop, length, function_call) and preserved role attribution on assistant messages.
Failure modes: if buffering exceeds configured threshold (default 2s or 1024 tokens), fall back to non-streaming error response with a clear OA-compatible error body and telemetry event.

Rollout: feature-flag gated. Canary plan: 5% of OA-compat traffic (hosted only) -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%. Dedicated and Private customers will receive an opt-in config in console for initial rollout. Gradual rollout ensures we can revert quickly if regressions appear.
tradeoffs_and_decisions: Chosen to prioritize client-compatibility over perfect low-latency in tool-calling flows. Rationale: tool calls must produce valid JSON events for downstream clients and webhooks, which requires buffering in the runtime.

Alternative considered: always emit intermediate 'delta' structured fragments and rely on client-side reassembly. Rejected because many legacy clients assume single function_call payload and will fail for partial JSON fragments.
Decision: implement a hybrid reassembly pipeline that minimizes buffering for common cases but guarantees structural correctness when function calls or JSON blocks appear.
Operational cost: added Redis dedupe store and additional tracing will increase infra usage; mitigations include TTL tuning and sampling on high-volume workloads.
testing_plan: Unit: translator mapping rules with randomized message sequences and edge cases (null fields, extremely long system prompts)
Integration: run a compatibility harness that replays recorded OpenAI traffic against the session weaver and compares envelope-by-envelope outputs
Load: synthetic streaming load to measure p99 latency and verify fallback thresholds under burst conditions
Canary E2E: deploy behind feature flag; monitor console dashboard and error budget for 48h before increasing traffic percentage
Compatibility matrix: test across SDK versions used by top 10 customers (list maintained in project doc)
rollout_and_monitoring: Canary schedule: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over 4 days with manual holds at each step.
Dashboards: console.redwood.ai/dashboards/compat-session-weaver (error rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, buffering events/sec, dedupe hits)
Alerts: high error rate (>1% spikes from baseline), increased buffering ratio (>10% of streams), unexpected increase in dedupe rejections (>0.5% per minute)
Postmortem: if any canary breach occurs, rollback and run RCA involving runtime, infra, and SDK owners
